table.brief: Link inventory: Page title / URL (long unbreakable URLs) / Last checked / Status code

conditions.browser: Chromium (Playwright build), macOS system fonts, deviceScaleFactor 1

candidates.name: s1A
candidates.idea: Move 15px from status to title while retaining the URL and date widths. Check whether the longer titles gain more natural breaks and whether the status header and codes remain comfortable at the narrower width.
candidates.label: gold

whys: The wider title column keeps the Salesforce title to two lines, while dates remain whole and URLs are readable. The status column is very tight around its two-line heading.
The wider title column keeps the Salesforce title to two lines, improving page lookup, while dates and status values remain whole. Long URLs still need up to four lines and the status header wraps.

The extra title width keeps the Salesforce title to two lines, while dates and status values remain whole. The status header fits on two lines, though its column is tight, and long URLs still require up to four lines.

candidates.name: d1r4B
candidates.idea: Preserve single-line dates and give URLs more space by testing a narrower title column. Check whether improved URL breaks compensate for taller titles.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Dates remain whole and the wider URL column improves several long links. The title column produces four lines for the Salesforce entry and fragments other titles more than D.
Dates stay whole and the wider URL column avoids some extra lines. The narrow title column makes several titles wrap to three or four lines, slowing page lookup.
The wider URL column improves several breaks and keeps dates whole. The tradeoff is a narrow title column: the Salesforce title takes four lines and the pricing title takes three.

candidates.name: d1r2A
candidates.idea: Keep complete dates for reliable scanning, while allowing the status header to wrap. Give the recovered width to titles, with the URL close to its current width.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Titles and dates scan well, and the URL column has useful space. The Salesforce URL puts a hyphen at the start of a line, while several URLs still require three or four lines.
Titles and dates scan well, with space allocated to the long URLs. The Salesforce URL has a line beginning with a hyphen, making that address slightly less continuous to read.
Titles and dates scan well, with a compact status column. The Salesforce URL has a less natural break before the hyphen in '-connector', and the first two URLs remain four lines tall.

candidates.name: d2r2A
candidates.idea: Keep the title and URL close to the stronger d2r1A proportions while giving Last checked enough room for one line. Accept a wrapped Status code header to preserve title space.
candidates.label: gold

whys: A useful balance: titles retain reasonably natural phrases, dates stay on one line, and the Salesforce URL breaks after its hyphen. Long URLs still wrap heavily, and the status heading takes two lines.
Titles are easier to scan than in A, and dates remain whole. The narrower URL column makes the first two addresses four lines tall, while the status header wraps cleanly.
Titles have useful room, dates stay whole, and URL words remain intact. The pricing title breaks naturally after 'and'; the first two URLs still require four lines.

candidates.name: d3r4A
candidates.idea: Test a wider title column while preserving complete dates and the URL minimum. The status header will wrap, but the extra title space may improve page lookup enough to justify the taller header.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Dates stay whole and the Salesforce URL breaks after its hyphen. The narrower title column splits the pricing title less naturally than in A or D.
Whole dates and compact status values are easy to scan. Titles have reasonable space, though the pricing title breaks less naturally than in D and the first two URLs need four lines.
Dates and codes are easy to scan, and URLs wrap without breaking words. The first two URLs occupy four lines, while several titles wrap over two or three.

candidates.name: contrast
candidates.idea: Equal columns give dates and status codes much more space than they need while leaving only 159 px of text width for URLs. The 324 px unbreakable URL unit would not fit without an additional break or overflow.
candidates.label: bad

whys: URLs are fragmented within domains and words, with up to eight lines in a cell. Single-line headings do little to offset the tall rows and unused space in the short-value columns.
The equal columns leave ample room around dates and codes while forcing URLs into many short fragments, including breaks within words. Tall rows make scanning and comparing records difficult.
The narrow URL column splits domains and path words across many lines. Tall rows and large empty areas under dates and codes make comparison laborious.
The wider URL column reduces wrapping, but every date splits across two lines and several titles become narrow stacks. Two wrapped headings reinforce the cramped right side.
The generous URL column helps long addresses, but every date splits after the year and both right-hand headers wrap. The narrow title column also produces lengthy title stacks.

The wide URL column gives several addresses more coherent lines, but every date splits after the year and both right-hand headers wrap. The narrow title column also produces several three- and four-line titles.
The narrow URL column breaks domains and path words across lines, making links difficult to inspect. Tall rows and large empty date and status cells make scanning inefficient.
URLs break repeatedly inside words and occupy up to eight lines, while the date and status columns have substantial unused space. The long rows weaken record-to-record comparison.
URLs fragment within words, including the careers and runbook paths. The resulting tall rows leave extensive empty space in the date and status columns.

d1.purpose: Audit a set of links by identifying each page, its destination, when it was checked, and the resulting status code.
tasks: Find a page by title and trace across its row to its URL, check date, and status.
Scan status codes to locate links that may need attention.
Compare check dates to identify stale results.
Read or verify a URL against its page title.
relations: Each row binds one page title to one URL, one check date, and one status code.
The date qualifies the status as the result of a particular check.
roles: Page titles identify entries; URLs identify their destinations.
Dates and status codes are compact audit results that support vertical scanning.
Headers name the four fields; all six body rows have the same structural role.
keep_whole: Individual words, date components, and status codes.
URL components where wrapping opportunities permit, especially the host and meaningful path segments.
may_wrap: URLs at available URL break opportunities; long destinations will need multiple lines.
Multiword headers when the space is better used for body content.
same_scale: All page titles share one column scale, and all URLs share another.
The two audit-result columns should both remain compact and easy to scan, though their widths need not be equal.
d1.h_vs_v: The URL needs the largest share of the width, but giving it more space makes titles or audit fields taller. Extra row height is acceptable when it preserves readable titles, recognizable URL segments, and scannable results.

d2.purpose: Audit a set of page links and their most recent check results.
tasks: Find a page by title and identify its URL.
Compare check dates and status codes to locate stale or problematic links.
Associate each URL and result with the correct page.
relations: Each row connects a page title to its URL, check date and status code.
The title and URL identify the resource; the last two columns describe its audit result.
roles: The header row names four fields; each subsequent row is one audited link.
Page titles are human-readable identifiers, while URLs provide precise destinations.
Check dates and status codes are compact comparison fields.
keep_whole: Meaningful URL components and long unbreakable identifiers where space permits.
Words and identifiers in page titles.
may_wrap: Page titles at natural word boundaries.
URLs at meaningful separators when supported by the rendering.
Dates between components if the chosen width requires it.
same_scale: All page titles share one column scale, and all URLs share another.
The two audit-result columns should remain compact and visually comparable.
d2.h_vs_v: Long URLs compete with page titles for a limited width. Extra row height can preserve readable titles and URL components, but excessive wrapping makes audit results harder to scan across rows.

d3.purpose: Audit a set of page links and their most recent check results.
tasks: Find a page by title or URL.
Associate each URL with its page, check date and status code.
Compare check dates and status codes across pages.
relations: Each row connects a page title and URL to the date and result of its link check.
The title and URL identify the same page; the date and status describe its check.
roles: The header row names four fields.
Each body row is one link record; the page title acts as a practical row identifier.
The date and status columns are compact lookup and comparison fields.
keep_whole: URL segments that cannot break naturally, including the longest 324px unit.
Words in page titles and headers.
may_wrap: Page titles at spaces and natural punctuation.
URLs at available break opportunities, while keeping unbreakable segments intact.
Multiword headers and dates at natural break points when space requires it.
same_scale: The date and status columns serve similarly compact audit fields, though the date needs more room.
Body rows share the same four-column structure even when their heights differ.
d3.h_vs_v: The URL needs a large minimum width to preserve its longest unbreakable segment; allocating more space to titles or compact audit fields reduces wrapping there but leaves URLs taller. Allowing vertical growth keeps the table within the viewport.

analysis.strengths: The page-title column supports readable phrases, dates and status codes are easy to scan, and the table fits the viewport without measured word breaks.
analysis.faults: The Status code header wraps, making the header row unusually tall. The Salesforce URL has a line beginning with a hyphen, which makes the address harder to follow.
analysis.spatial_logic: P gives the title more room than R or S, keeps the date wide enough for its header, and assigns most remaining space to URLs.

analysis.strengths: Titles retain useful phrases, dates and codes scan cleanly, and the Salesforce URL wraps more naturally than in P. The table fits with no measured word breaks.
analysis.faults: Status code wraps to two lines, and the longest URLs still take four lines. Several URL lines split the domain or path across visually separate fragments.
analysis.spatial_logic: Q transfers two pixels from the title and status columns to the URL. That small change improves a URL break while preserving P's row heights and most of its title wrapping.

analysis.strengths: All headers fit on one line, producing a compact, clear header row. Dates and status codes remain easy to compare, and the URL width matches Q's.
analysis.faults: The narrow title column fragments several titles: Salesforce Connector Configuration Reference takes four lines, and the pricing title takes three. This makes page lookup slower and increases the pricing row's height.
analysis.spatial_logic: R gives status enough space for its complete header by taking width from page titles. The shorter header is offset by a taller body row, so overall height remains unchanged.

analysis.strengths: The widest URL column reduces the first URL to three lines and keeps more of the Salesforce URL together. The body rows have a comparatively regular rhythm.
analysis.faults: The title column breaks several names into short fragments, including a four-line Salesforce title. The status header still wraps, so the wider URL comes at a noticeable cost to page lookup.
analysis.spatial_logic: S prioritizes the long addresses, funding their extra width mainly from the title column. A shorter first data row balances a taller pricing row, leaving total height unchanged.

analysis.strengths: Titles are generally readable, dates and codes scan clearly, and URLs get the same width as in Q. It fits without measured word breaks.
analysis.faults: Status code still wraps despite receiving more width than in Q. The pricing title breaks before 'and Plan Comparison', while long URLs remain four lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: T gives a few more pixels to status than Q and slightly fewer to titles, without gaining a single-line status header or changing the measured row heights.

rounds.insights: The main tradeoff is between recognizing page titles and following long URLs. Q preserves useful title phrases while giving URLs enough width for a cleaner Salesforce break than P. R shows that a one-line status header is possible, but its cost to title readability is substantial. S shows that extra URL width can save a line, though the resulting title fragmentation limits the benefit. All five fit the viewport and have the same total height, so height alone does not distinguish their reading quality.

analysis.strengths: The table fits the viewport, and dates and status codes are easy to scan. The wider URL column keeps the links readable without measured breaks inside words.
analysis.faults: The narrow title column creates several short lines, including four lines for the Salesforce title. The pricing title takes three lines and makes that row taller than its URL requires.
analysis.spatial_logic: Most width goes to the long URLs, while the date and status columns remain compact. That allocation leaves the titles slightly too constrained.

analysis.strengths: The wider title column improves several breaks and lets the pricing row fit in two lines. Dates and codes remain aligned and scannable, and the table fits the viewport.
analysis.faults: The first two URLs still occupy four lines, and some titles remain fragmented. The status column has more space than its values need, while its header still wraps.
analysis.spatial_logic: Moving 10px from URL to title improves the title column and reduces one row’s height without increasing the measured maximum line count or introducing word breaks.

rounds.insights: Layout Q makes better use of the available width: a small gain in the title column improves reading and removes a line from one row. The URL column is already at the measured minimum needed for its longest unbreakable unit, while the status column may have a little width to spare.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport with all dates and status codes visible. Page titles wrap at natural word boundaries, and the Salesforce title remains on two lines. The URL column accommodates the longest unbreakable unit.
analysis.faults: Long URLs require up to four lines, and the Status code header wraps onto two lines. The Legacy API title takes three lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: The URL receives the most space, while the date column is just wide enough for its header. The compact status column leaves more room for page titles.

analysis.strengths: Also fits the viewport, preserves the same row heights, and keeps dates and status codes easy to scan. Its wider status column gives that heading more breathing room.
analysis.faults: The extra status width does not prevent its header from wrapping. The narrower title column pushes the Salesforce title onto three lines without reducing any row height.
analysis.spatial_logic: Moving 15 px from the title to the status column adds space where the short codes do not need it, while making a long title harder to read.

rounds.insights: Both layouts give URLs and dates the same width and have the same overall height. The comparison favors allocating the remaining space to titles: in s1A it improves a title break, whereas the wider status column in Q does not change its header or values.

contrast.why: Equal columns give dates and status codes much more space than they need while leaving only 159 px of text width for URLs. The 324 px unbreakable URL unit would not fit without an additional break or overflow.

synthesis.rationale: s1A gives page titles enough room to make them easier to scan, while retaining a wide URL column and keeping dates and codes intact. Layout S makes a different, comparable tradeoff: its wider URL column shortens the first URL to three lines and keeps the second to three, at the cost of more fragmented titles. Both fit the viewport and preserve the table's structure.

general: Allocate width according to content and lookup tasks, including headers and padding.
Judge actual line breaks and row relationships in the rendered table, not just width or height metrics.
Keep dates, codes and meaningful text units intact where possible.
specific: The URL column needs substantially more width than either audit field.
The 117 px date column keeps the header and dates on one line.
A two-line status header can be a reasonable exchange for more space in the title or URL column.

synthesis.tradeoffs: s1A favors scanning page titles; S favors reading URLs. R keeps every header on one line but narrows the title column, while P, Q and T make smaller variations on the title-versus-URL balance. s0A is taller because its narrower title column adds a line to the pricing row.
synthesis.uncertain: The preferred finalist depends on whether readers more often locate entries by page title or inspect URLs. The judgments assume the rendered breaks remain stable at the specified font and viewport.

critique.good: All content fits, both audit fields stay on one line, and the compact header and aligned dates and codes make scanning straightforward.
critique.problems: Several titles take three or four lines, and most URLs split their hostnames and long path segments across lines. The result is dense in the identifying fields, with unused space below the short audit values.
critique.cause: The 150px title column and 345px URL column are constrained by the 117px date and 107px status columns.

critique.good: The 390px URL column reduces wrapping in some destinations, while status codes remain easy to scan. All content fits.
critique.problems: Every date breaks after the year, making date comparison slower; both audit headers also wrap. Titles remain narrow, and some URLs still split hostnames.
critique.cause: The 85px date column is too narrow for a complete date, and the 84px status column wraps its header. The 160px title column leaves longer titles fragmented.

critique.good: The wider title column makes page names easier to recognize and reduces wrapping in several rows. Status codes remain easy to scan, and all content fits.
critique.problems: Every date breaks after the year, both audit headers wrap, and the URLs still split hostnames and long paths. The tall header and short third body row create a less even rhythm.
critique.cause: The 200px title column takes space from the audit fields, leaving the date at 87px and status at 87px; the URL remains at 345px.

critique.good: The title column supports relatively natural phrases, and the status codes form an easy-to-scan column. All content fits the viewport.
critique.problems: The last three dates split across lines, making date comparison uneven. Both audit headers wrap, and several URLs break within the host or across long path segments.
critique.cause: The 105px date column is too narrow for every complete date; the 84px status column wraps its header. The 345px URL column forces several destination breaks.

critique.good: The wider URL column reduces some destinations to three lines and keeps more path text together. Status codes remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: The title column produces a four-line Salesforce title and fragments other titles. The last three dates split, and both audit headers wrap. Several hosts still break across lines.
critique.cause: The 160px title column is narrow, while the 105px date column cannot hold every date. The 84px status column wraps its header; the 370px URL column still cannot keep every host whole.

critique.good: All dates and headers stay on one line, making the audit results particularly easy to scan. Status codes align consistently, and the table fits the viewport.
critique.problems: The narrow title column fragments several titles, particularly the four-line Salesforce entry. URLs frequently break within hosts and across path segments, and the wider status column leaves unused space beside short codes.
critique.cause: The 150px title column and 345px URL column constrain the identifying fields, while 107px is devoted to keeping the status header on one line.

critique.good: Titles are relatively easy to scan, dates and codes stay on one line, and the pricing row is compact. No measured word breaks occur.
critique.problems: Most URLs split their hosts across lines, making destinations harder to verify. The two-line status header makes the header row disproportionately tall.
critique.cause: The 343px URL column leaves limited room for long URL components; the 84px status column is too narrow for its header on one line.

critique.good: The wider URL column keeps the Salesforce path break at a hyphen, while dates and status codes remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: The narrow title column fragments several titles, including Salesforce into four lines. The pricing title adds a line even though its URL needs only two. The status header wraps.
critique.cause: The 160px title column is too narrow for comfortable title lookup; the 84px status column wraps its header.

critique.good: The wider title column gives titles clear, mostly natural breaks, and the audit results remain scannable.
critique.problems: The Salesforce URL breaks inside 'salesforce', and the pricing URL takes an extra line. Most hosts still split across lines, and the status header wraps.
critique.cause: The 333px URL column is too narrow for a long unbreakable URL unit; the 84px status column wraps its header.

critique.good: All headers fit on one line, the compact audit fields scan cleanly, and no measured word breaks occur.
critique.problems: Several titles are fragmented across three or four lines, slowing page lookup. The wider status column leaves substantial unused space below its header, while most URL hosts still split.
critique.cause: The 150px title column constrains page names; the 107px status column reserves width mainly to keep its header on one line.

critique.good: Titles remain reasonably compact, status codes are easy to scan, and URL wrapping avoids breaks inside words.
critique.problems: Every date splits before the day, making date comparisons slower. Several hosts also split across lines.
critique.cause: The 100px date column is too narrow for the complete dates; the 360px URL column cannot keep every host and path segment together.

critique.good: The wider URL column gives the first two destinations more continuous path text, and the first three dates fit on one line.
critique.problems: The other three dates wrap, producing an inconsistent date column. Several titles become unusually tall, including a four-line title, weakening row scanning.
critique.cause: The 105px date column falls close to the date width threshold, while the 165px title column sacrifices too much space to the 368px URL column.

critique.good: Titles are reasonably compact, status codes scan easily, and the status header fits on one line.
critique.problems: Every date wraps, and the Salesforce URL breaks inside a word. The single-line status header does little to improve the audit task.
critique.cause: The 100px date column is too narrow, and the 337px URL column forces an internal word break; the 107px status column uses space that could serve those fields.

critique.good: All dates fit on one line, making comparisons easy. Titles remain reasonably compact, status codes align clearly, and URL words are not broken internally.
critique.problems: The Salesforce URL wraps immediately before a hyphen, making its path slightly harder to follow. Several hosts split across lines, and the status header wraps.
critique.cause: The 343px URL column is constrained by the space needed for titles and complete dates; the 84px status column accommodates the codes but not their full header on one line.

critique.good: The title column keeps most titles in two or three readable lines. The URL has enough space to retain many useful path segments, and status codes scan cleanly.
critique.problems: The last three dates split across lines, making date comparison harder. Both audit headers wrap, and several URLs split their hosts or leave short fragments on a final line.
critique.cause: The 105px date column is too narrow for every date and its header. The 359px URL column still forces some host and path breaks.

critique.good: All dates and the date header stay on one line, making the audit results easy to scan. The wider URL column reduces wrapping in the first two destinations.
critique.problems: The title column makes several titles unnecessarily tall, especially the four-line Salesforce title. Hosts still split in most URLs, and the status header wraps.
critique.cause: The 155px title column is restrictive; the 365px URL column is still too narrow to keep several full hosts together. The 82px status column cannot hold its header on one line.

critique.good: Titles have a more comfortable measure than in d1r4B, while every date and the date header remain on one line. Status codes align clearly.
critique.problems: The narrower URL column creates four-line destinations in the first two rows and leaves a leading hyphen on one URL line. Several hosts split, and the status header wraps.
critique.cause: The 343px URL column places breaks at awkward points. The 84px status column leaves some width available that could instead support the URLs.

critique.good: All headers and dates stay on one line, making the audit results easy to scan. URLs avoid the measured word breaks, and the table fits the viewport.
critique.problems: Several titles take three or four lines, making page lookup slower and leaving the first two rows particularly dense. Long URLs also require substantial vertical reading.
critique.cause: The 150px title column is narrow, while the 117px date and 107px status columns preserve one-line labels and dates.

critique.good: The 190px title column makes most page names easier to read, and the 345px URL column avoids the measured word breaks. The table fits the viewport and has the same overall height as A.
critique.problems: Every date splits before the day, making date comparisons harder. Both audit headers wrap, increasing the header height; the detached day numbers also weaken the otherwise orderly scan down the result columns.
critique.cause: The 102px date column is too narrow for a complete date, and the 82px status column is too narrow for its header.

critique.good: The wider title column keeps several page names to one or two lines and makes them easy to find. Status codes remain visible and aligned.
critique.problems: Dates split across lines, both audit headers wrap, and URL identifiers break inside words, including salesforce and incident. The additional URL wrapping also makes the table taller.
critique.cause: The 225px title column takes space from the URL and audit columns; 324px is insufficient for the longest unbreakable URL unit plus padding, and 90px is insufficient for a complete date.

critique.good: Fits the viewport with complete dates and status codes. The wider title column keeps several page names in compact, natural groups, and the pricing row is especially easy to scan.
critique.problems: Both audit headers wrap, making the header disproportionately tall. Several URLs break the hostname across lines, and the longest destinations occupy four lines.
critique.cause: The 111px date and 85px status columns are too narrow for their headers; the 345px URL column limits how much of each destination can stay together.

critique.good: Dates and codes remain intact, and the URL column has slightly more room. The table fits without horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Both audit headers still wrap. Several titles take more lines than in d2r1A, including the pricing title, which adds a line to that row. The extra height weakens the scan across audit results.
critique.cause: The 165px title column loses useful space, while the increases to the 349px URL and 95px status columns do not visibly offset that loss.

critique.good: All four headers fit on one line, creating a compact header. Dates and codes remain whole, and the table fits the viewport.
critique.problems: The narrow title column fragments several page names into three or four lines, making titles harder to locate. Long URLs still occupy up to four lines and often split the hostname.
critique.cause: The 150px title column is constrained by allocating 117px and 107px to the date and status columns, while the URL column remains at 345px.

critique.good: Titles are relatively easy to scan, dates and codes stay on one line, and the pricing row is compact. All content fits.
critique.problems: The two longest URLs take four lines, and the status header wraps, making the header as tall as a short data row.
critique.cause: The 345px URL column limits long paths; the 83px status column cannot accommodate its full header.

critique.good: The wider URL column reduces the first long URL to three lines and keeps more of the second URL together. Dates and codes remain easy to compare.
critique.problems: Several titles become fragmented, including a four-line Salesforce title and a three-line pricing title. The status header still wraps.
critique.cause: The 150px title column gives up too much space to the 369px URL column; the status column is 83px.

critique.good: Titles retain the readable wrapping of d2r2A, and all dates and codes remain whole.
critique.problems: Both audit headers wrap, while the wider title and status columns bring no visible improvement over d2r2A. Long URLs still occupy four lines.
critique.cause: Reducing the date column to 111px wraps its header; 85px is still too narrow for the status header.

critique.good: All headers, dates and codes fit on one line, producing a compact header and clear audit columns.
critique.problems: The narrow title column makes several page names harder to scan, while the two longest URLs still take four lines. The result is a dense body below a much shorter header.
critique.cause: The 150px title column and 345px URL column share the space remaining after allocating 117px and 107px to the audit columns.

critique.good: Both audit headers and all dates fit on one line. Page titles are generally easy to scan, and the result columns are clearly separated.
critique.problems: The URL column breaks words in the Salesforce and incident-response paths. The first two rows are tall, while the result columns contain substantial unused space.
critique.cause: At 325px, the URL column is too narrow for some path segments; the 117px and 107px result columns leave less room for URLs.

critique.good: The wider URL column avoids measured breaks inside words and keeps every row to three lines or fewer. Page titles retain useful word groupings.
critique.problems: Every date splits before its day, making date comparisons slower. Both audit headers wrap, and the narrow result columns look compressed beside the URL column.
critique.cause: The 98px date column cannot hold a full date, and the 78px status column cannot hold its header on one line.

critique.good: Dates stay whole, titles are readable, and URLs have no measured breaks inside words. The compact status column preserves space for the identifying fields.
critique.problems: The status header wraps and makes the header row taller. The first two URLs still need four lines, leaving substantial empty space in their result cells.
critique.cause: The 83px status column is narrower than its header, while the 345px URL column cannot accommodate the longest paths in fewer lines.

critique.good: Both audit headers and dates fit on one line, and URLs have no measured breaks inside words. The result fields are easy to scan.
critique.problems: Several page titles fragment across three or four lines, making page lookup slower. The first two rows remain tall despite the narrow title column.
critique.cause: The 150px title column sacrifices useful title groupings to give the status column 107px.

critique.good: Titles are relatively easy to scan, dates and codes stay on one line, and the pricing row is compact. All content fits within the viewport.
critique.problems: Both audit headers wrap, while the first two URLs occupy four lines and several hostnames split across lines.
critique.cause: The 110px date and 84px status columns are too narrow for their headers; the 351px URL column cannot keep several long URL components together.

critique.good: The wider URL column reduces the first two URLs to three lines and keeps more of their paths together. Dates and codes remain easy to compare.
critique.problems: The Salesforce title takes four lines, and the pricing title takes three, making page lookup more labored. Both audit headers wrap.
critique.cause: The 160px title column gives space to the 369px URL column; the 110px date and 80px status columns do not accommodate their headers on one line.

critique.good: The status header, dates, and codes stay on one line, and the table fits the viewport.
critique.problems: The narrow URL column produces four-line URLs in the first two rows, with a hyphen starting a line in the second URL. Several titles also wrap heavily, and the table is taller than the other designs.
critique.cause: The 107px status column uses space that would help the 338px URL and 164px title columns; the 110px date column still wraps its header.

critique.good: The date header and values stay on one line, titles are comparatively readable, and the pricing row is compact. The table fits the viewport.
critique.problems: The status header wraps, and the first two URLs take four lines, splitting hostnames and long paths across lines.
critique.cause: The 83px status column is too narrow for its header, while the 345px URL column has limited room for long destinations.

critique.good: All content fits within the viewport. Dates, status codes and headers stay on one line, and the wider URL column keeps several addresses to three lines.

d2r0A.idea: Protect the longest URL unit and keep both audit headers on one line, accepting substantial wrapping in page titles.

d2r0B.idea: Preserve the longest URL unit while giving titles more room by allowing the compact audit fields and headers to wrap.

d2r0C.idea: Prioritize scanning page titles and accept more URL and audit-field wrapping to distribute space more evenly across identification and results.

d3r0A.idea: Give the URL the greatest feasible width while keeping the date and status fields on one line, accepting narrow, more heavily wrapped page titles.

d3r0B.idea: Balance title readability with single-line audit fields, using the minimum width that accommodates the longest unbreakable URL unit.

d3r0C.idea: Prioritize recognizable page titles and the minimum viable URL width, allowing the date and status headers and dates to wrap more often.

d1r0A.idea: Keep both audit columns wide enough for their measured one-line contents while giving the URL its longest unbreakable unit and letting titles wrap.

d1r0B.idea: Favor URL inspection with the widest destination column, accepting more wrapping in titles and compact audit columns.

d1r0C.idea: Favor finding pages by title while retaining enough URL width for its longest unbreakable unit and using compact, similarly scaled audit columns.

d2r1A.idea: Test a wider title column while retaining the URL width that avoided word breaks. Give the date column enough room for the measured 90px date text and padding, accepting a wrapped status header to improve title readability and keep dates whole.

d2r1B.idea: Test a more balanced compromise: preserve whole dates and provide slightly more URL space, while giving titles more room than A. The status header may wrap, but its codes remain compact.

d1r1A.idea: Give titles 35px more than A while retaining the same URL width. Allocate enough room for complete dates and accept a wrapped status header to improve title recognition without breaking date values.

d1r1B.idea: Test a more URL-focused balance while keeping dates whole. The wider URL column may preserve more meaningful destination segments, with a modest improvement in title width over A.

d3r1A.idea: Give titles 30px more while preserving the minimum URL width and single-line dates. Let the status header wrap; its three-digit values should remain intact. Test whether better title scanning justifies the taller header.

d3r1B.idea: Test a wider URL column with compact audit fields and a modest increase over A's title width. This may reduce URL wrapping while avoiding some of A's most fragmented titles.

d2r2A.idea: Keep the title and URL close to the stronger d2r1A proportions while giving Last checked enough room for one line. Accept a wrapped Status code header to preserve title space.

d2r2B.idea: Test whether a meaningfully wider URL column improves hostname and path wrapping. Keep Last checked on one line and allow Status code to wrap, with the narrower titles as the tradeoff.

d1r2A.idea: Keep complete dates for reliable scanning, while allowing the status header to wrap. Give the recovered width to titles, with the URL close to its current width.

d1r2B.idea: Keep complete dates and use a wrapped status header to give URLs more room, testing whether improved destination wrapping outweighs the narrower titles.

d1r2C.idea: Prioritize natural title phrases and complete dates, testing the readability cost of a narrower URL column.

d3r2A.idea: Test a middle ground between d3r0B and d3r1B: give URLs 10px more while preserving single-line audit headers. Check whether URL wrapping improves enough to justify the narrower titles.

d2r3A.idea: Test whether a more readable title column and single-line headers outweigh the extra URL wrapping caused by a narrower URL column.

d2r3B.idea: Test a wider URL column while retaining the stronger title width. Allow both audit headers to wrap and check whether dates remain whole at 98px.

d3r3A.idea: Give the title 12px from the status column while retaining the URL minimum and the single-line date header. Test whether improved title grouping justifies wrapping the status header.

d3r3B.idea: Test a wider title column by allowing both compact audit headers to wrap naturally. Check that dates remain whole and that the taller header is offset by clearer titles and shorter body rows.

d1r3A.idea: Keep the strongest title width and give the URL 17px more by narrowing the date column. Test whether dates remain whole and URL breaks improve.

d1r3B.idea: Test a larger URL allocation while retaining more title space than d1r0A. The compact audit columns should still accommodate their body values; check their headers and date rendering.

d1r3C.idea: Test the clearer title scale with a single-line status header, using a narrower date column. Check whether the reduced URL width introduces word breaks or less recognizable URL segments.

d2r4A.idea: Keep the readable title scale and compact status column, while giving the URL a little more room. Test whether 110px still keeps dates and their header whole.

d2r4B.idea: Test the wider URL scale that kept paths to three lines in d2r3B, while reserving enough room for whole dates. The narrower title and wrapped status header are the tradeoffs to inspect.

d2r4C.idea: Test whether a moderate title width and a slightly wider URL than d2r3A can preserve whole words while keeping both audit headers on one line.

d3r4A.idea: Test a wider title column while preserving complete dates and the URL minimum. The status header will wrap, but the extra title space may improve page lookup enough to justify the taller header.

d3r4B.idea: Test a smaller transfer from status to titles. This may improve title breaks while keeping dates whole, with the tradeoff of a likely two-line status header.

d1r4A.idea: Keep the stronger title width, give the URL more room, and test whether 105px is sufficient for all dates with the revised allocation. The existing render suggests some dates may still wrap.

d1r4B.idea: Preserve single-line dates and give URLs more space by testing a narrower title column. Check whether improved URL breaks compensate for taller titles.

d2r5A.idea: Give titles a little more room while retaining the single-line date header; check whether the narrower URL column changes important breaks.

d2r5B.idea: Test a wider URL column with the single-line date header, looking for shorter URL blocks without the most severe title wrapping seen in d2r4B.

d2r5C.idea: Test a single-line status header while preserving the more readable title width; assess whether the narrower URL column costs too much in height and continuity.

s1A.idea: Move 15px from status to title while retaining the URL and date widths. Check whether the longer titles gain more natural breaks and whether the status header and codes remain comfortable at the narrower width.
